newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan eases censorship on foreign newspapers.
newsitem.headline: Jordan eases censorship on foreign newspapers.

text.p: Jordan has eased censorship on foreign newspapers entering the country, Information Minister Marwan Muasher said on Thursday.
Muasher said the government had cancelled a requirement for the newspapers to be checked before distribution in Jordan for possible violations of the country's stringent Press and Publications Law.
Newspaper vendors say the monitoring process delayed distribution and often led to foreign papers being pulled from the market.
Muasher said decision took effect earlier this week.
"This is the first step," Muasher told Reuters. "The next will be a revision of the law to minimise constraints on publications."
The law currently sets out a wide range of no-go subjects for books and newspapers. They include:
-- news that offends King Hussein or the royal family;
-- articles that contain contempt of religion;
-- articles that damage national unity or encourage crime;
-- articles that shake confidence in the Jordanian dinar;
-- news reports or articles contrary to public morals or ethics.
One newspaper distributor said the Egyptian magazine Rose el-Youssef, which often focuses on themes of Zionism and sex, often fell foul of the law and was repeatedly banned.

Many local journalists have also run into trouble. The Arab Organisation for Human Rights in Jordan said on Wednesday between 20 and 25 journalists were taken to court last year over newspaper articles.
Muasher said until the law was amended the government would continue to deal with any infringements by foreign publications.
"If there are violations we will notify the concerned publications and make sure it does not reoccur," he said.
